attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡  Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡  Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: create new sprite kind, game set up, sprite creation, sprite events, game over.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a new sprite kind inside the SpriteKind namespace at the top of the editor?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the new sprite kind be used for in the project? 

❓ How do you create a new sprite kind in JavaScript?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When naming new sprite kinds, it’s important that the ninja uses UpperCamelCase. This uses the same convention as camelCase, but the first letter is capitalized.

💡 A namespace is a separate section of code inside curly brackets { }. The namespace will help organize code in a project, similar to code comments. 

💡 Walk through the syntax of the code that declares a new sprite kind with the ninja. Make sure that they have included the correct keywords, symbols, functions, and spacing so that the new sprite kind is able to be used outside of the namespace.
steps.instructions:
Create a new sprite kind for an Insect sprite under the comment // create new sprite kind.


Access the SpriteKind namespace by typing the keyword namespace then SpriteKind and a pair of curly brackets { } 


To use the new sprite kind outside of the namespace, start with the keyword export then use let, the name of the new sprite kind, Insect, an assignment operator, and the SpriteKind.create() function to create a new sprite kind within the namespace.


Use UpperCamelCase, and capitalize the first letter of the new sprite kind name, too.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a Player sprite, set its starting position, enable it to be controlled by direction buttons, and set it to stay in screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image might you use for the Player sprite?

❓ What might happen to the Player sprite in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the x-coordinate range (0-160) and y-coordinate range (0-120) when setting the Player sprite’s position.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // sprite creation. Select a Player sprite image from the gallery or My Assets and update the sprite name.


Position the Player sprite on the bottom center of the screen. Open Sprites again, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the Player sprite creation code, and update the x and y parameters. 


Allow the Player sprite to move all around the screen. Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the position code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name.


Keep the Player sprite in screen. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) stay in screen (true)] underneath the Player sprite movement code. Update the sprite name, and use the default argument true.


Click ▶ to move the Player sprite around the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a for loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How was a [for] loop used in the blocks editor? Did any other loops perform similar actions?

❓ How many times will the for loop run? How do you know?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the [repeat] and [for index] loops in the blocks editor. Both of these loops repeated code for a set number of times. In JavaScript, there is no repeat loop, instead only the for loop is used for this purpose.

💡 Walk the ninja through each of the expressions inside the parentheses of the for loop. The initialization expression sets an initial value for the counter variable. The run condition expression sets the condition that needs to be true, in order for the loop to run. The increment expression sets the value that the counter variable will change by after each iteration of the loop. 

💡 The default expressions will begin the counter variable at 0 and run while the counter is less than 5. Because the increment increases the counter variable by 1 after each iteration, the loop will run 5 times (0, 1, 2, 3, 4).
steps.instructions:
Use a for loop to create multiple sprites at once!


Open Loops and drag [for] underneath the Player sprite code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { }

The for loop has 3 expressions, separated by semicolons ; inside the parentheses: initialization, run condition, and increment. 


The initialization expression let i = 0 will declare the counter variable and set its initial value. In this case, the counter i will be set to 0. 


The run condition expression i < 5 will continue running the loop while the condition evaluates to true. In this case, the code in the loop will run while the counter is less than 5. 


The increment expression i++ is used to update or increment the counter variable. The increment operator ++ adds 1 to the counter variable after each iteration of the loop. Based on the three expressions, this loop will run a total of 5 times.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag  setPosition, setVelocity, and setBounceOnWall inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the for loop runs?

❓ How do you change a sprite kind in JavaScript?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Each time the for loop runs, an Insect sprite will be placed in a random position, its velocity will be set, and it will bounce on walls. Because the for loop runs 5 times, there will be 5 Insect sprites on screen, all behaving the same way.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the for loop has its own set of curly brackets { }. This means that the for loop will only iterate through code placed inside of its block statement.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can update the sprite kind by deleting .Player then retyping the dot operator . and selecting Insect from the list of properties.
steps.instructions:
Add code inside the for loop to create 5 moving Insect sprites!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop. Select an insect sprite from My Assets and update the sprite name. Update the sprite kind with the new kind created for the Insect sprite in the SpriteKind namespace.


Set the Insect sprites to appear in random positions. Open Sprites again, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] inside the for loop, underneath the code that creates the Insect sprite. Update the sprite name and use randint to randomize the x and y-positions.


Set the velocity of each Insect sprite when it is created. Open Sprites again, drag [set (mySprite) velocity to vx vy] inside. Update the sprite name and tinker with the vx and vy parameters to make the Insect sprites move diagonally across the screen.


Make each Insect sprite bounce when it hits a wall. Open Sprites again, drag [set (mySprite) bounce on wall] inside. Update the sprite name and keep the default argument set to true . 


Click ▶ to see 5 Insect sprites appear in random positions on screen, move around, and bounce on walls!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the run condition expression so that the for loop creates 7 Insect sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does changing the run condition impact how many Insect sprites are placed on the screen? 

❓ What would you do if you wanted fewer Insect sprites to appear on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the run condition expression sets the condition that needs to be true in order for the loop to run. By changing the condition’s value, the loop will run while the counter variable is less than 7. This value can be changed to increase or decrease the number of times that the loop will run.
steps.instructions:
Update the expressions in the for loop to add more Insect sprites!


The run condition expression i < 5 currently runs the code in the for loop’s block statement while the counter variable is less than 5. Since the counter variable begins at 0 and increases by 1 on each iteration, the loop creates 5 Insect sprites.


Replace 5 with 7 to run the code 7 times, creating 7 Insect sprites when the loop runs. 


Click ▶ to see 7 Insect sprites appear in random positions on screen, move around, and bounce on walls!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the kind parameter to Player and otherKind parameter to Insect in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps with an Insect sprite?

❓ How many points might the Player sprite earn when it overlaps an Insect sprite?

❓ Why should otherSprite be used in the setPosition code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps with an Insect sprite, a certain number of points will be added to the score and the Insect sprite’s position will be reset. 

💡 otherSprite should be used in the setPosition code so that the Insect sprite (which is used as the otherKind parameter) has its position reset on overlap.
steps.instructions:
Score a point when the Player sprite overlaps with an Insect sprite!


Open Info and drag [set score to (value)] underneath // game set up. Leave the default argument set to 0. 


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // sprite events. Leave the kind parameter as Player. Change the otherKind parameter to Insect.


Open Info again and drag [change score by (1)] inside the curly brackets { } of the Player/Insect sprite onOverlap event. Tinker with the score value to set how many points the Player sprite will earn on overlap with an Insect sprite.


Reset the Insect sprite to a random position on the screen when it is “caught” by the Player sprite. Copy (Ctrl + C) the Insect sprite’s setPosition code from the for loop and paste (Ctrl + V) it underneath the changeScoreBy code, then replace the sprite name with otherSprite.

 

Click ▶ to see the Player sprite score a point when it overlaps an Insect sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the countdown in info.startCountdown, then use quotation marks to separate the strings from the variables in showLongText?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How long might the countdown timer be set for?

❓ Does the dialog box message appear as it was intended? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the project to make sure the strings and number values they’ve concatenated appear correctly when the dialog box shows.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
Set a countdown timer, then reveal the score when the timer reaches 0!


Open Info and drag [start countdown (10) (s)] under // game set up, then update the time parameter to set the amount of time the user has to catch Insect sprites.


Open Info and drag [run code on countdown end] under // game over. Then open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] inside the curly brackets { } of onCountdownEnd. 


In the parentheses, replace null by concatenating strings and the value of info.score() to tell the user how many Insect sprites they caught. Update the layout parameter, too.


Last, open Game and drag [game over (true)] under the dialog box code to end the game. Update the win parameter to true. Add an effect, too.


Click ▶ to see the number of Insect sprites caught appear on screen after the timer runs out.

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help players understand how the game is played?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should otherSprite be used in the startEffect code?

❓ What background image might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 otherSprite should be used in the startEffect code so that the Insect sprite (which is used as the otherKind parameter) starts an effect. 

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding effects, a background image, and directions!


Open Sprites and drag [(mySprite) start (effect) effect] underneath the changeScoreBy code. Replace the sprite name with otherSprite, then use the dot operator . to select an effect that matches the sprite’s image. Add a short duration parameter, too. 


Open Scene, drag [set background image to (img)] under // game set up.  Click the palette to choose a background image from the Gallery.


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath the startCountdown code under // game set up. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.


Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.title: Fireflies Collector
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses a for loop to create multiple sprites at once!

validationItems.text: Create a new SpriteKind named Insect.
Create a sprite, give it the Player SpriteKind, set its position, and move it with the controller.
Write a for loop and update its run condition expression so it runs 7 times.
Inside the for loop, create a sprite, give it the Insect SpriteKind, give it a random position and a random  velocity, and set it to bounce on the wall.
Set the score and increase it whenever the Player sprite overlaps an Insect sprite.
Create a countdown timer. When it ends, display a message containing the user’s score and then end the game.
Add effects, a background image, and instructions for the user.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about for loops. Using for loops, you can code things to happen multiple times. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Getting Loopy
badges.description: Control how a loop runs using its 3 expressions in JavaScript.

badges.title: Here We Go Again
badges.description: Write a for loop that starts at zero and counts up using an increment operator.

badges.title: Where it Stops, Nobody Knows
badges.description: Write a for loop that runs a random number of times.

badges.title: Sugar, We’re Going Down
badges.description: Write a for loop that starts with a number larger than zero and counts down using a decrement operator.

badges.title: Double the Fun
badges.description: Nest a for loop inside another for loop.

badges.title: Memory Palace
badges.description: Save the game’s high score.

badges.title: Trophy Room
badges.description: Display the high score to the user.

badges.title: Depth Perception
badges.description: Set a sprite’s z-position so it appears in the front of a scene.
